name: Zinc Grey
lede: Zinc Grey takes its name from the dull, bluish-grey sheen of the metal zinc, distinct from zinc white, the pigment made from zinc oxide.

sections.title: The metal, not the pigment
sections.body:
Zinc Grey is filed under our pigment-and-mineral names simply as the color of the metal zinc itself, rather than of zinc white, the opaque pigment painters have used since the nineteenth century [1]. Our sources give no date for when the color name itself entered use [1].

Its nearest look-alikes are [[grebe]], 2.8 units away, and [[greyish-umber]], 2.9 units away, both almost the same; [[plain-mouse]], at 3.0, is also close [2]. Other systems file the same region as Dark Greyish Brown or Dusky Drab [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The color appears in 4.52 percent of 23,781 paintings, 1,076 of them as photographed, more common than 84 percent of the names we track [3]. Eugène Louis Boudin used it most, in 4 of 15 works here, 4.8 times his museums' baseline [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, found in 5.6 percent of the 1,674 paintings we have from then, 94 of them, 1.8 times the expected rate, and plays a mid-tone in 35 percent of its paintings [3]. The earliest dated match goes back to 1119, though the archive's early centuries are thin enough that this is a floor, not a first [3].
